title: Where is…?
topic: אֵיפֹה; directions (יָשָׁר, יָמִינָה, שְׂמֹאלָה); places in town
why: First lesson of the "In Town" unit: asking where a place is, understanding directions, and saying whether it's near or far. It reuses יֵשׁ, the article, and adjective agreement from units 4 and 5.

{"lessons": ["

Excuse me, where is…?

To stop someone in the street, you start with סְלִיחָה (slikha, excuse me), then ask your question with אֵיפֹה (eifo, where?). As always in the present tense, there is no verb \"to be\": you say \"where the-bank?\"

סְלִיחָה, אֵיפֹה הַבַּנְק?Excuse me, where is the bank? [slikha, eifo ha-bank?]

Looking for a bank, any bank? Then you ask whether there is one, with יֵשׁ:

סְלִיחָה, יֵשׁ פֹּה בַּנְק?Excuse me, is there a bank here? [slikha, yesh po bank?]
אֵיפֹה יֵשׁ מִסְעָדָה?Where is there a restaurant? [eifo yesh mis'ada?]

Watch out: \"where is a restaurant?\" doesn't work in Hebrew any more than it does in English. With the article הַ, it's a specific place; without the article, you use יֵשׁ (\"is there…?\").

", "

Straight ahead, right, left

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
יָשָׁרyasharstraight ahead
יָמִינָהyaminato the right (rightward)
שְׂמֹאלָהsmolato the left (leftward)
וְאָזve'azand then, next
לְיַדleyadnext to

The final ה of יָמִינָה and שְׂמֹאלָה shows direction: \"toward the right,\" \"toward the left.\" In שְׂמֹאלָה, the dot on the left makes an s (sin) and the א is silent: you simply say \"smola.\"

יָשָׁר, וְאָז יָמִינָה.Straight ahead, and then right. [yashar, ve'az yamina.]
הַבַּנְק לְיַד הַשּׁוּק.The bank is next to the market. [ha-bank leyad ha-shuk.]

Israelis often give directions with no verb at all: \"straight ahead, and then left.\" These little words are all you need.

", "

Is it near or far?

קָרוֹב (near) and רָחוֹק (far) are adjectives: they agree with the place, like גָּדוֹל / גְּדוֹלָה.

MasculineFeminine
nearקָרוֹב karovקְרוֹבָה krova
farרָחוֹק rakhokרְחוֹקָה rekhoka
הַשּׁוּק קָרוֹב, וְהַתַּחֲנָה רְחוֹקָה.The market is near, and the stop is far. [ha-shuk karov, ve-ha-takhana rekhoka.]

With זֶה, you stay in the masculine: זֶה קָרוֹב? (is it near?). For distance, people count in minutes, using the number forms you already know: חָמֵשׁ דַּקּוֹת בָּרֶגֶל (five minutes on foot).

And if you don't know? אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ (a man) / אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדַעַת (a woman): I don't know. Or אֲנִי לֹא מִפֹּה: I'm not from here.

Every Israeli town has its שׁוּק (market): it's often the best landmark when you ask for directions.
